newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Major says Asia's poor need free markets.
newsitem.headline: Major says Asia's poor need free markets.

text.p: British Prime Minister John Major criticised Western nations on Saturday for failing to open their markets enough, saying the poor of Asia and the rest of the world could only benefit if there was free trade.
After a tour of a village 65 km (40 miles) north of Dhaka which is receiving British aid, he said trade was far more effective than aid alone to help lift people out of poverty.

"I think frankly there is something immoral in Western Europe and the large wealthy countries providing aid resources with one hand but closing their markets to those countries with the other hand," he told an impromptu news conference.

"If they open their markets, then a great deal more good could be done," said Major after announcing four million pounds ($6 million) of development aid for projects in Bangladesh, already the second biggest recipient of British aid after India.

Major and his wife, Norma, were clearly moved by their reception in the village, where they saw leather and silk-spinning workshops, as well as a credit union helping women build up small businesses and a small school.
Villagers lined the dusty streets and the canal banks to applaud and shout greetings as he passed, and local women presented him with a hand-made bedspread as a leaving gift.

The visit was the showpiece of Major's one-day stay in Bangladesh, which this year celebrates its 25th anniversary of independence from Pakistan and which is struggling to build up an economy hit by natural disasters and political upheavals.
Major also laid a wreath at the memorial for independence war heroes and held talks with Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and her bitter opposition rival, Begum Khaleda Zia.
He also witnessed the signing of a $150 million contract between Petrobangla and Britain's Cairn Energy to jointly develop the Sangu offshore gas field in the Bay of Bengal.

Major's tour of Bangladesh, Pakistan and India, where he was mobbed by wellwishers and feted by the media, is designed to boost trade and forge long-term commercial contacts in a region which has the potential to become an economic powerhouse.
But he has been criticised at home by ruling Conservative members of parliament for going on a week-long foreign trip just as the battle for the looming election enters its final phase.
Major, undaunted by an opposition Labour Party opinion poll lead of some 20 points with the election now no more than four months away, has rejected such criticism.

But domestic politics have continued to intrude. The British media have interpreted some of his speeches as a pitch for the ethnic Indian, Pakistani and Bangladeshi vote at home, where it could tip the balance in marginal parliamentary seats.

Major leaves on Sunday for Pakistan, where he will hold talks with government and opposition leaders as well as travel to the Khyber Pass, the legendery gateway to the subcontinent defended by British troops in the heyday of Britain's empire.
